blocks.text: Every earlier lesson in this module described one piece of the machine, sessions, transports, ids, state. This lesson puts all of those pieces back together and follows a single tool call on its full round trip, from the moment a host decides it needs an answer, through a client instance and a transport, into a server and back again. Seeing the whole path at once is what makes the earlier, more isolated lessons click into a single coherent picture.
1. The Full Path at a Glance

blocks.alt: A host, client, transport, and server form the full request path

blocks.text: A single tool call crosses six architectural boundaries before an answer comes back, host to client, client to transport, transport across the wire, transport to server, server back to transport, and transport back to client, host. None of these steps are optional, and skipping past any of them in a mental model tends to be exactly where confusing bugs come from later.

blocks.title: Six components, not four
blocks.content: It is tempting to collapse this to host, client, server, but the transport appears twice, once on each side of the connection, and deserves to be counted separately since it is where bytes actually travel and where framing and connection failures actually happen.

blocks.text: It helps to number these boundaries explicitly the first time through, because most descriptions of MCP gloss over several of them at once, saying simply the host calls the tool, which quietly hides four or five real architectural handoffs behind one casual verb.
2. Step One: The Host Decides to Call a Tool

blocks.alt: A host decides to call a tool

blocks.text: The flow begins inside the host, not the client, the host, driving the overall conversation, decides based on the current task and the model's output that a specific tool needs to be called with specific arguments. At this point nothing has been sent anywhere yet, this is purely a decision made using the conversation state described in State Management.

This decision often comes from a language model's output requesting a specific tool by name with specific arguments, but the mechanism is the same regardless of what triggered it, the host is the component responsible for deciding that an external call is needed at all.

Nothing about MCP itself constrains how this decision gets made, that logic belongs entirely to the host and whatever reasoning process drives it, MCP only becomes involved once the decision has already been made and needs to be carried out.
3. Step Two: The Host Selects the Right Client Instance

Because a host may be connected to several servers at once, it first has to determine which client instance actually owns the tool being called, using the aggregated tool listing it maintains across all connected servers. This routing decision happens entirely inside the host, the chosen client instance is not consulted about whether it is the right one, the host already knows.

This selection step is exactly where the tool aggregation and collision-avoidance concerns discussed in Multi-Server Architecture come into play, if two servers happened to expose tools with the same name, this is the step where that ambiguity would have to already be resolved.

blocks.title: A lookup, not a negotiation
blocks.content: Selecting the client instance is a simple lookup against state the host already maintains, it is not a negotiation with the client or server, by the time this step happens the host already knows exactly which server owns the requested tool.

blocks.text: 4. Step Three: The Client Builds the Request

The chosen client instance takes the tool name and arguments from the host and wraps them into a properly formed JSON-RPC request, generating a fresh id and recording that id in its pending-requests map, exactly as described in Client-Server Communication.

At this point the client instance owns the request completely, the host has handed off responsibility, and everything that happens for the rest of this flow, until a result comes back, is the client's job to track correctly.

Building the request correctly here matters more than it might seem, an id collision or a malformed params object at this step propagates all the way through the remaining twelve steps before anyone downstream has a chance to catch it.
5. Step Four: The Client Hands the Message to the Transport

The client does not know or care whether this session runs over a subprocess pipe or a network connection, it simply calls the transport's send operation with the serialized message, exactly the narrow interface described in Transport Layer, and the transport takes over from there.

This handoff is a clean architectural boundary, the client serializes a JSON-RPC message, the transport serializes that into bytes on the wire, and neither side needs to know anything about the other's internal implementation beyond the narrow send and receive interface.

It is worth noting the client never inspects what transport it is using to decide how to format its message, the JSON-RPC message is built identically whether it will travel over a pipe or a network connection next.
6. Step Five: The Transport Carries the Bytes

The transport frames the message appropriately for whichever channel it is, a newline-delimited line on a pipe, an HTTP request body over a network, and delivers it toward the server. This is the one step in the entire flow that has no idea what tools/call even means, it only knows it is moving bytes reliably from one side to the other.

If this step fails, a dropped connection, a crashed subprocess, the transport surfaces a close or error event, which the client-side logic uses to reject any pending requests immediately rather than waiting on a timeout that may take much longer to fire.

It is worth remembering this step never inspects the message content at all, whatever framing rule the transport applies wraps around the JSON-RPC text without parsing it, the transport is finished with its job the moment the bytes are delivered intact.
7. Step Six: The Server-Side Transport Reassembles the Message

On the server's side, its own transport implementation reads the incoming bytes, reassembles a complete frame, and hands the parsed JSON-RPC message upward to the server's request-handling logic, again without inspecting or caring what the message means.

A malformed frame at this step, truncated bytes or invalid JSON, is where the server transport itself would raise an error, before the message even reaches the request router, this failure mode is entirely local to the transport and never involves the tool handler at all.

Once reassembled, this raw parsed message is the exact same JSON object the client built back in step three, nothing about its content changed anywhere along the journey, only its representation as bytes on the wire did.
8. Step Seven: The Server Routes to the Correct Handler

blocks.alt: A server routes to the correct handler

blocks.text: The server looks at the method field, tools/call, and the tool name inside params, and routes the request to whichever internal handler is registered for that specific tool. If no handler exists for that name, the server responds immediately with an error rather than attempting anything further.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field inspected","Used for"],"rows":[["method","Which category of operation, tools/call, resources/read, and so on"],["params.name","Which specific tool or resource within that category"]]}

blocks.text: This routing table is typically built once, when the server starts up and registers its tools, rather than being reconstructed on every incoming request, keeping this step fast even under heavy concurrent load.
9. Step Eight: The Server Executes the Tool Logic

The matched handler actually runs, using only the arguments provided in this request, consistent with the stateless design covered in State Management. This is the one step in the whole flow where real work happens, everything before it was routing the request there, everything after it is routing the answer back.

If the handler raises an error partway through, that error is caught at this step and turned into a JSON-RPC error response in the next step, rather than propagating as a raw exception that would leave the request unanswered.

Everything the handler needs was supplied in the request's arguments, consistent with the stateless design covered in State Management, it does not reach back into any memory of earlier calls to do its work.
10. Step Nine: The Server Builds the Response

Once the handler produces a result, or an error, the server wraps it in a JSON-RPC response carrying the identical id from the original request, nothing else identifies which call this response answers, the id is the only link.

An error outcome is built the same way, still carrying the original id, just with an error field instead of a result field, since correlation by id has to work identically whether the call succeeded or failed.
Building the response is the last step that happens purely on the server side, everything from here on is about getting that already-finished answer back to whoever asked for it.
11. Step Ten: The Response Travels Back Through the Transport

blocks.alt: A response travels back through the transport

blocks.text: The response makes the same journey in reverse, framed by the server-side transport, carried across the same channel, and reassembled by the client-side transport, which hands the raw parsed message upward without any awareness of what it contains.

Notice this step is the mirror image of step five, the same transport implementations, the same framing rules, just carrying data in the opposite direction, there is no separate response-only channel or special case for the return trip.
12. Step Eleven: The Client Matches the Response to Its Request

The client looks up id 42 in its pending-requests map, finds the entry created back in step three, and resolves it with this response's result, exactly the mechanism described in Client-Server Communication. If no matching entry existed, perhaps because the request already timed out, the response is discarded instead.
13. Step Twelve: The Client Hands the Result to the Host

Resolving the pending entry triggers whatever callback the host originally registered when it made the call, and the result flows back up into the host's handling of the current conversation turn, closing the loop that started in step one.

The client's job at this point is done, it has correctly correlated a response to its request and handed the result upward, everything about what the host does with that result next is entirely outside the client's concern.
14. Step Thirteen: The Host Incorporates the Result

blocks.alt: A result gets incorporated into the host answer

blocks.text: The host adds the tool result to its conversation state and continues, perhaps calling another tool, perhaps generating a final answer for the user. This is where the request-response flow formally ends, the same host that started the cycle is the one that closes it.

This is the step that closes the loop opened in step one, the host now has the information it was missing, and the overall conversation can move forward, whether that means calling another tool, asking the user a follow-up question, or producing a final answer.
15. Where Things Can Go Wrong Along the Way

Each of the thirteen steps above is also a place something can fail, a transport can drop the connection mid-flight, a server can return an error instead of a result, a client can time out waiting for a response that never arrives. A robust host treats every one of these as a normal outcome to handle, not an exceptional case to ignore.

blocks.title: Failure at any step still produces a resolution
blocks.content: Whether the outcome is a successful result, an error response, or a timeout, the pending-requests entry created in step three always gets resolved one way or another, the host is never left with no idea what happened to its call.

blocks.text: 16. Many of These Flows Happen at Once

Nothing about this thirteen-step path assumes it is the only one happening, a host frequently has several of these flows in progress simultaneously, some to the same server, some to different servers entirely, each tracked independently by its own id and its own pending-requests entry, exactly as covered in Client-Server Communication.

This is precisely why the pending-requests map from Client-Server Communication is keyed by id rather than assumed to hold exactly one entry, a busy session might have a dozen of these thirteen-step flows overlapping at any given moment, each perfectly isolated from the others by its own id.

Understanding the flow as a single thirteen-step trace does not conflict with this concurrency, it simply means many such traces can be interleaved in time, each one internally still following the exact same thirteen steps in the exact same order.
17. Worked Example: Tracing One Call End to End
Follow a single search tool call through every component it touches.

items: 1. Host decides to call the search tool with a query.
2. Host looks up which client instance owns the search tool and selects it.
3. Client builds a tools/call request with id 42, records it in its pending-requests map.
4. Client sends the request to its transport.
5. Transport frames and delivers the bytes to the server.
6. Server transport reassembles the message and passes it to the request router.
7. Server matches method and tool name, invokes the search handler.
8. Handler runs the search and returns a result.
9. Server wraps the result in a response carrying id 42.
10. Server transport sends the response back across the same channel.
11. Client transport reassembles it and hands it to the client logic.
12. Client finds id 42 in its pending-requests map and resolves it.
13. Host receives the result and continues the conversation.

blocks.text: Notice how closely this thirteen-step trace matches the numbered sections above it, that is deliberate, each section describes exactly one line of this trace in more depth, and the trace is what ties them back together into a single, ordered story.
18. Common Mistakes When Reasoning About the Flow

items: Assuming the client talks directly to the server, skipping over the transport's actual role in between.
Forgetting that routing to the correct client instance happens inside the host, before the client is ever involved.
Treating the transport as if it understands tool names or arguments, when it only ever sees bytes.
Assuming one request-response flow blocks all others, instead of recognizing many can run concurrently.
Not handling the case where a response never arrives, leaving the host waiting indefinitely on a call that will never resolve.

blocks.text: A surprising number of integration bugs trace back to a mental model that silently skipped a step, usually the transport, treating a client and server as if they spoke to each other directly tends to produce debugging effort aimed at the wrong layer entirely.
Writing out the full trace, as the worked example above does, is one of the most effective ways to catch this kind of oversimplified mental model before it causes a real debugging headache.
19. Practice: Diagram Your Own Tool Call

Pick any tool call from a system you are familiar with and write out its own thirteen-step trace, labeling exactly which component, host, client, transport, or server, is responsible for each step, then check whether any step you wrote skips a component that should actually be involved.

code.content:
1. Host decides: ...
2. Host selects client: ...
3. Client builds request: ...
...
13. Host incorporates result: ...

blocks.text: If your trace has fewer than thirteen distinct steps, look specifically for a step you merged together that should really be two, most commonly the client-to-transport handoff and the transport-to-server delivery collapsed into a single imagined direct call.
Key Takeaway

A single tool call is really a thirteen-step relay across host, client, transport, and server, and back again, with each component doing exactly one narrow job and nothing more, the host deciding and routing, the client tracking and matching, the transport moving bytes, and the server executing and responding.

This lesson traced one flow between one host and one server. The next lesson, Multi-Server Architecture, looks at what changes when a host is running many of these flows against many different servers at the same time.
